messages:
alex_support: Heads-up — ACME private deployment hitting KMS failures since 09:12 UTC. Customer sees repeated: "error: dial tcp i/o timeout" when our control plane tries to reach their on-prem HSM. Request IDs: req=6c9b3f, 6c9b41. They say this started after a firewall rule change on their border router.

luca_support: Adding logs from the control plane (trimmed):
```
 2026-02-18T09:12:03Z control-plane KMS: dial tcp 10.11.5.23:443: i/o timeout
 2026-02-18T09:12:27Z control-plane KMS: retrying connection (attempt 2)
 2026-02-18T09:12:59Z control-plane KMS: handshake failed: tls: oversized record received with length 20527
```

raj_sre: Thanks. Two quick suspects: DNS resolving to wrong IP (internal NAT/proxy) or TLS SNI/cert mismatch. Also possible SNAT port exhaustion if they changed border rules. Can we get a tcpdump from the customer's egress and a dig from the control-plane node?

emma_ops: I asked customer to run these from their gateway node (they gave ephemeral access):
```
dig +short kms.acme.internal @10.11.0.2
# -> 10.11.5.23

curl -v --resolve "kms.acme.internal:443:10.11.5.23" https://kms.acme.internal/health
# shows TLS alert: handshake_failure

openssl s_client -connect 10.11.5.23:443 -servername kms.acme.internal -showcerts
# connects then spits: "140735...: TLS alert: handshake failure"
```

chris_infra: They also shared a short tcpdump capture from their egress NAT box (trimmed):
```
09:11:59.123 IP 10.2.4.12.52000 > 10.11.5.23.443: Flags [S], seq 12345, win 64240
09:12:03.456 IP 10.2.4.12.52000 > 10.11.5.23.443: Flags [S], seq 12346, win 64240 (retrans)
09:12:27.789 IP 10.2.4.12.52000 > 198.51.100.7.443: Flags [S], seq 22345
```

chris_infra: Note there is an unexpected destination 198.51.100.7 in one of the flows — could be their HA pair or an intermediate proxy. That suggests DNS or a split-horizon resolver returning different A records intermittently.

raj_sre: Also check the customer's egress firewall for TLS intercept / outbound proxy. The TLS alert + oversized record sometimes means an HTTP proxy returned a plaintext HTTP response on port 443. Ask: do they run a TLS-terminating proxy that requires CONNECT?

alex_support: I asked customer: do you have a corporate proxy / TLS inspection device? They said they recently deployed a Palo Alto outbound rule that forwards traffic to an inline proxy for inspection. They said rules were tightened yesterday.

emma_ops: That aligns. Two actionable repros for them to run and paste back:
1) curl with verbose to both IPs we saw (10.11.5.23 and 198.51.100.7):
```
curl -v --connect-to :kms.acme.internal:10.11.5.23 https://kms.acme.internal/health
curl -v --connect-to :kms.acme.internal:198.51.100.7 https://kms.acme.internal/health
```
2) tcpdump filtered on the source port used by our control-plane (they can map from our logs) and capture the HTTP initial bytes. If they see HTTP/1.1 400 from proxy that's a smoking gun.

luca_support: Customer ran the commands and returned this: first IP -> TLS handshake_failure, second -> HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden from "InspectProxy/1.2". They confirm the inline proxy responds with 403 because the SNI doesn't match a configured allowlist.

raj_sre: OK root cause: outbound TLS inspection/proxy returning HTTP (oversized record) and blocking SNI values. The control plane attempts to reach the HSM using target host "kms.acme.internal" and SNI set to that name; the proxy requires explicit allowlisting of that SNI or IP.

chris_infra: Remediation options we gave the customer:
- Add kms.acme.internal to the proxy's TLS allowlist / bypass for 10.11.5.23 and 198.51.100.7 IPs.
- If proxy cannot be bypassed, configure the proxy to forward CONNECT to the HSM (no MITM) for the control-plane subnet.
- As a temporary workaround, set control plane to use direct peering IP (if they can NAT to a dedicated IP) and ensure SNI matches.

emma_ops: Also noted: their HSM vendor cert uses CN=kms.acme.internal but vendor requires client TLS with specific ALPN. We recommended they ensure the proxy preserves SNI and ALPN bits when forwarding, otherwise handshake fails. We sent them a config snippet for Palo Alto: allowlist based on destination host header + enable TLS passthrough for 10.11.5.0/24.

alex_support: Customer applied a bypass rule for our control-plane CIDR and retried. Their tests now:
```
curl -v --resolve "kms.acme.internal:443:10.11.5.23" https://kms.acme.internal/health
# -> HTTP/200 OK

# Control plane log after change:
2026-02-18T09:45:11Z control-plane KMS: connected to 10.11.5.23:443, TLS handshake complete
```

luca_support: Customer confirms production traffic restored, no more 504s or dial timeouts. They will keep the bypass but update their proxy config to be less restrictive for KMS maintenance windows.

raj_sre: Postmortem notes for us (to add to ticket):
- Cause: corporate TLS inspection/proxy returned plaintext HTTP for blocked SNI -> TLS handshake failure / oversized record.
- Contributing: recent firewall rule change and absence of SNI allowlist entry for kms.acme.internal.
- Mitigation: recommend customers with on-prem HSMs to add control-plane CIDRs and kms hostnames to egress bypass, or enable TLS passthrough for HSM IPs.
- Long-term: add additional health-check fallback in control plane to surface proxy-detected HTTP responses (e.g., detect "InspectProxy" server header) and create clear error code for SNI/proxy block.

chris_infra: I'll file a follow-up RFC to add a phase in our KMS connectivity check that validates server cert CN and detects proxy plaintext responses earlier.

alex_support: Marking thread resolved with customer — they said thanks. :tada: Ticket #INC-5487 will remain open for doc updates.

hsm_bot: Automated note: scheduled task KMS-rotate-cert (customer=ACME) deferred due to connectivity event; will retry in 24h.
